author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
Fixes https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/28909

`HivePartitioning::ApplyFiltersToFileList` copied every filter for every
file, substituted the file's partition values as constants and evaluated
the result with `ExpressionExecutor::TryEvaluateScalar`. That creates a
new `ExpressionExecutor` per (file, filter), so functions with expensive
local state rebuild it for every file - e.g. `day()`/`month()`/`year()`
build a 29,584-entry `DateLookupCache` each time, making pruning ~10x
slower than with `dayofmonth()`.

This PR evaluates each filter with a single executor over all files:

* The partition/filename column references of each filter are rewritten
once into `BoundReferenceExpression`s into an input chunk (replacing
`ConvertKnownColRefToConstants`).
* The partition/filename values of all files are loaded as (unescaped)
strings into a VARCHAR `DataChunk`, one row per file, and the column
references are wrapped in a cast to the partition type, so no `Value` is
created per file and the cast runs as part of the filter. The filter is
run with `SelectExpression` per `STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE` batch.
`SelectExpression` is used rather than `ExecuteExpression` since some
internal table filter functions (e.g.
`__internal_tablefilter_selectivity_optional`) only have a select
callback.
* Whether a filter can be evaluated on partition values only (no
volatile functions, parameters, subqueries, other columns, ...) is still
decided by the existing `IsScalar()`/`IsFoldable()` check, done once per
filter.
* If evaluating a batch throws (e.g. a cast that fails for some
partition values), the batch is split in halves recursively, so only the
files for which the filter throws are kept (and the filter is preserved)
while the other files are still pruned. A single bad value costs
~2*log2(2048) extra evaluations for its batch only. A partition value
that cannot be cast to its `hive_types` type therefore no longer errors
during pruning - the scan still raises the same `Unable to cast ...
(from hive partition column ...)` error when it reads the file, unless
another filter prunes that file.
* The NULL marker / unescape handling is shared with
`HivePartitioning::GetValue`.
* The order of `file_filters` and of the preserved filters is unchanged.

#### Timings (10,000 hive partitions, none match, reldebug)

| filter | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| `day(date) = 40` | 2.32 s | 0.22 s |
| `month(date) = 13` | 2.12 s | 0.23 s |
| `year(date) IN (1990, 1991)` | 1.24 s | 0.21 s |
| `dayofmonth(date) = 40` | 0.78 s | 0.22 s |

Added `test/sql/copy/partitioned/hive_partition_filter_evaluation.test`,
covering date part pruning, mixed partition/regular column filters,
volatile filters, filters that throw for some partitions, cast errors,
escaped values, NULL markers and filename filters, and
`hive_partition_filter_evaluation_large.test_slow`, which checks that
one throwing partition value among 2100 files still prunes the rest of
its batch (6/2100 files scanned).

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
hunk_contexts: void DatabaseHandle::Read(QueryContext context, FileBuffer &block, uint64_t loca
message:
A block id that is stored in the metadata of a database file is used
without looking at it. Two cases, both hit by `ATTACH` of a corrupt
file:

* The pointer to the next block of a metadata chain holds a very large
block id. `SingleFileBlockManager::GetBlockLocation` multiplies the id
with the block size, which wraps around. `DatabaseHandle::Read` then
decides whether the read can be served from the prefetched header with
`location + block.AllocSize() <= prefetched_header->size()`. That sum
wraps as well, the check passes, and one block is copied from outside of
the prefetched header buffer. AddressSanitizer reports the read; a
release build reports a checksum mismatch over whatever memory was
copied (the numbers in the message differ from run to run).
* The list of metadata blocks that is stored with the free list holds a
block id in the range of in-memory blocks: `INTERNAL Error:
AddAndRegisterBlock called with a transient block id`, which invalidates
the instance.

With this PR:

* `GetBlockLocation` throws `Data Corruption Error: Corrupt database
file: block id <id> is out of range` when the location of the block or
its end does not fit.
* The check in `DatabaseHandle::Read` no longer adds to the location.
* `MetadataManager::Read` throws `Data Corruption Error: Corrupt
database file: invalid metadata block id <id>` for an id that is
negative or in the range of in-memory blocks.

A block id that is in range but past the end of the file is not touched
here: reading it already fails with a regular error.

### Test

`test/sql/storage/corrupt/block_id_out_of_range.test` attaches one file
per case (`data/storage/corrupt/block_id_location_overflow.db.gz`,
`metadata_block_id_transient.db.gz`, 4 KB and 3 KB) and checks that the
instance is still usable afterwards. Both files were found by fuzzing
the storage reader. The test also passes under AddressSanitizer, which
reported the out-of-bounds read for the first file before the fix.

Note: this PR was generated by an AI coding agent.

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
## The query shape

A correlated `EXISTS` (or correlated `IN`) whose subquery also carries a
predicate on the outer key only:

```sql
SELECT ... FROM orders o
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.customer_id > 17000);
```

This is what query generators and hand-written reports produce when a
restriction on the outer row is written next to the correlation instead
of in the outer `WHERE`: the two places are equivalent for `EXISTS`, and
a view or a template often only allows adding conditions inside the
subquery. Written in the outer `WHERE`, the predicate is pushed into the
scan of `orders`. Written inside the subquery it is not: the outer rows
are produced in full and the predicate is only applied to the
duplicate-eliminated domain.

## What happens today

The subquery is decorrelated into a materialized CTE of the outer rows
with two references: the outer rows on the left side of a MARK join, and
the domain of distinct keys below the subquery. The predicate
`o.customer_id > 17000` ends up as a filter on the domain reference
only. The CTE filter pusher restricts a CTE only when every reference is
filtered, so the scan of `orders` stays unfiltered:

```
CTE __duckdb_delim
  SEQ_SCAN orders  [customer_id, amount]                                ~3,000,000 rows
  FILTER  SUBQUERY
    HASH_JOIN  MARK; customer_id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM customer_id
      CTE_SCAN                                                          ~3,000,000 rows
      ... HASH_JOIN INNER customer_id = customer_id
            (GROUP BY over FILTER (#[0.0] > 17000) over CTE_SCAN)
            SEQ_SCAN customers  Filters: customer_id > 17000
```

## The change

The change lives in the CTE filter pusher. Before it pushes the filters
of the references into a CTE, it treats a join that keeps only the
matching rows of a CTE reference as one more consumer filter of that
reference:

```
SEMI[l = r](CTE_REF c, R)                 ->  SEMI[l = r](FILTER[p(l)](CTE_REF c), R)
FILTER[mark](MARK[l = r](CTE_REF c, R))   ->  FILTER[mark](MARK[l = r](FILTER[p(l)](CTE_REF c), R))
                                              when p(r) is TRUE for every row of R
```

A left row survives a SEMI join, or a MARK join under a filter on the
bare mark, only together with a right row whose key equals its own. A
comparison with constants that is TRUE for the key of every right row is
therefore TRUE for the key of every surviving left row, and filtering
the left side by it first removes only rows that the join drops anyway.
With the filter on the outer rows' reference every reference of the CTE
is filtered, and the pusher moves the predicate into the CTE definition
as it does for any other consumer filter:

```
CTE __duckdb_delim
  SEQ_SCAN orders  [customer_id, amount]  Filters: customer_id > 17000  ~600,000 rows
  FILTER  SUBQUERY
    HASH_JOIN  MARK; customer_id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM customer_id
      FILTER (#[0.0] > 17000)
        CTE_SCAN
      ... (unchanged)
```

It is built from three parts:

- **Orchestration: `CTEFilterPusher::GenerateSemiJoinFilters`**, called
from `CTEFilterPusher::Optimize` right after it has collected the CTEs
and their references (implemented in
`src/optimizer/cte_semi_join_filter_transfer.cpp`). It uses the pusher's
own reference inventory to decide whether a reference qualifies (every
other reference of the CTE is filtered already) and records the new
filter there, so the push that follows sees an ordinary filtered
reference. It is part of the `cte_filter_pusher` optimizer and is
switched off with it.
- **Discovery: which filters hold for every right row.** A small search
follows the right join key down through filters, table filters of a
scan, column-reference projections, the groups of an aggregate, the
preserved side of joins and the equalities of INNER joins, and collects
the filters that compare that column with constants. It does not look at
the left side and does not rewrite anything. The positive-MARK case is a
separate check (`FILTER` with the bare mark as a conjunct over a MARK
comparison join) that only selects the join.
- **Transfer: `FilterCombiner::GenerateJoinFilters`**, unchanged, the
helper that `FilterPullup::PullupSemiJoin` and
`FilterPushdown::PushdownSemiAntiJoin` use. It derives the left-side
filters from the collected right-side filters and the join conditions;
the search also uses it for the equalities of an INNER join. Which
predicates can cross an equality is therefore decided in one place:
comparisons with constants, `BETWEEN` and `IN` lists (as
`FilterCombiner::GetComparedExpression` defines them). Predicates the
helper does not derive (`OR`, `IS [NOT] NULL`, `NOT IN`) are not
transferred.

`CTEFilterPusher::PushFilterIntoCTE` is unchanged. It restricts a CTE by
the disjunction of the filters of its references and hands that to the
expression rewriter, whose `DistributivityRule` reduces `(A AND B) OR A`
to `A`. The new filter usually repeats the filter of the other
reference, so it is added to the plan as one flat conjunction, which is
the form the rule reduces; the scan then gets `customer_id > 17000` and
not a disjunction. Nothing else simplifies the pushed filter, for any
CTE.

## Preconditions

- The left child of the join is a reference of a materialized CTE (bare
or under a filter), not a recurring or correlated reference, and every
other reference of that CTE is already filtered. The new filter is then
exactly what the CTE filter pusher was missing. Other left sides (for
example a plain table scan under an uncorrelated `IN`) are left alone.
- A SEMI comparison join, or a MARK comparison join directly under a
filter that has the bare mark as a conjunct. Not ANTI, outer, delim or
AsOf joins, and not a mark that is used in any other way (`NOT mark`,
under an `OR`, in the select list).
- The join condition is `=` or `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`, with a bare
column on the right side.
- Only filters that compare the key with constants and cannot throw are
transferred: comparisons, `BETWEEN` and `IN` lists. A function of the
key, an `OR`, a NULL test and `NOT IN` are not.
- "Every right row passes it" is established conservatively: the
NULL-extended side of an outer join, grouping sets, set operations, CTE
references and optional scan filters end the search.

## Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders AS
    SELECT i AS order_id, (i * 7919) % 20000 AS customer_id, DATE '2024-01-01' + (i % 365)::INTEGER AS order_date,
           ((i % 1000) / 10.0)::DECIMAL(10,1) AS amount, 'note ' || (i % 100000) AS note,
           i % 7 AS status, i % 13 AS channel, i % 101 AS store_id
    FROM range(30000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE customers AS SELECT i AS customer_id, 'customer ' || i AS name, i % 50 AS region FROM range(18000) t(i);

SELECT status, channel, count(*), sum(amount), max(note), min(order_date), max(store_id)
FROM orders o
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND <predicate on o.customer_id>)
GROUP BY status, channel;
```

Base of this branch against the branch, release builds. User-mode
instructions of a single-threaded run (`perf stat -e instructions:u`,
median of 3, including the 0.24 G of process start-up):

| predicate inside the subquery | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `o.customer_id > 17000` (15 % of the rows pass it, 5 % have a match) |
13.5 G | 5.8 G |
| `o.customer_id BETWEEN 100 AND 300 AND c.region < 25` | 13.1 G | 4.2 G
|
| `o.customer_id > 100000` (no row can match) | 9.4 G | 0.26 G |
| control: `o.customer_id > 17000` written in the outer `WHERE` | 4.5 G
| 4.5 G |

The control shows what is left on the table: with the predicate in the
outer `WHERE` the subquery is deliminated into a plain semi join. The
change does not rewrite the query into that form, it only stops the scan
from producing rows that cannot match.

## Regression check

None of the TPC-H and TPC-DS queries has this shape, so the two suites
are regression evidence only and the example above carries the case.
Base against branch at SF1:

- plans: 0 of 121 queries change;
- results with 1 and with 16 threads: identical (one query differs in
the last digit of a floating-point aggregate between two parallel runs
of the same binary);
- `scripts/plan_cost_runner.py` on `benchmark/tpch_plan_cost`: no
differences.

## Tests

`test/optimizer/cte_semi_join_filter_transfer.test` (434 assertions): 42
result cases over tables with NULL, duplicate and unmatched keys on both
sides (empty left / right side, null-safe correlation, `NOT EXISTS`,
`EXISTS` as a value, the mark under an `OR`, a predicate that can throw,
the NULL-extended side of a LEFT join, grouping sets, `UNION`, nested
`EXISTS`, correlated `IN`, VARCHAR and DATE keys, DOUBLE keys with
`0.0`, `-0.0` and NaN, references of a materialized CTE whose filters
differ only in the sign of a zero passed to `signbit`, query-written
materialized CTEs with one reference, a reference that is filtered
already, two filtered references and one unfiltered reference) and 24
plan pins: the predicate reaches the outer scan as a single filter for
`>` (also with a negative zero and under a null-safe correlation),
`BETWEEN`, `IN` lists, a second correlated column, a correlated `IN` and
a reference that is filtered already; it does not for `NOT EXISTS`, a
mark that is output or under an `OR`, a plain scan on the left side, a
function of the outer key, an `OR` or a NULL test on the key, the
NULL-extended side of an outer join, grouping sets, a CTE with an
unfiltered reference, and with the CTE filter pusher disabled. A last
block repeats result cases with the CTE filter pusher disabled.

Existing tests: no expected plan or result changes. `test/optimizer/*`,
`test/sql/cte/*`, `test/sql/subquery/*`, `test/sql/join/*` and
`test/sql/filter/*` pass, also with column binding verification, forced
external operators, forced storage and forced row fetches.

This PR touches `cte_filter_pusher.cpp` in one place (the call of the
helper) and adds one source file.

Relation to #28760 / #28639: those PRs change the filter dependency of
delim CTEs in the other direction and remove identity projections around
them; the plan pins of this test need to be re-run once they land.
Relation to #28732: once `FILTER[mark](MARK)` is a SEMI join by the time
the CTE filter pusher runs, the MARK check here is dead and can be
removed; the SEMI case covers it.

Note: this PR was generated by an AI coding agent.

author: Mark <mark.raasveldt@gmail.com>
message:
A smaller alternative to duckdb/duckdb#28639. It fixes the same two v2.0
regressions after delim joins became materialized CTEs: a lateral UNNEST
runs out of memory, and a `json_valid` guard stops protecting a lateral
table function in a correlated subquery. It uses the same two planner
changes as duckdb/duckdb#28639 and leaves out the third.

**Kept from duckdb/duckdb#28639**
- `CanRestrictCorrelationDomain` now accepts `LOGICAL_UNNEST` and table
in-out functions that are not volatile and have no final step. The CTE
filter pusher can then move a guard on the outer rows into their input.
This alone fixes the Malformed JSON errors for `range`, `unnest` and
`json_each`.
- The rewrite no longer wraps its two CTEs in identity projections
(added in eb35d40269c for column pruning, which `RemoveUnusedColumns`
now handles for materialized CTEs). A filter that can throw therefore no
longer stops at a projection that isn't a query block boundary, and
reaches the UNNEST output. This fixes the OOM. duckdb/duckdb#28639 used
a projection flag for this instead.

**Left out**
- Running `EMPTY_RESULT_PULLUP` again after statistics propagation,
together with the anti-join projection-map change it needs. On main this
case already takes about 0.01 s (3M rows, the view example in
duckdb/duckdb#28639). The extra pass also changed which errors get
raised, and it forced edits to 4 unrelated tests (`deliminator.test`,
`scalar_aggregate_merge_tpcds_plan.test`, `test_window_self_join.test`,
`updating_the_join_node_hash_map_has_no_errors.test_slow`). None of
those tests change here.
- The two new test files are merged into one,
`test/sql/subquery/lateral/lateral_filter_into_delim_cte.test`, without
`PRAGMA enable_verification`. The file is skipped under
`verify_serializer` and `disable_optimizer`, as in duckdb/duckdb#28639,
because both drop the planner-only marks.

**Extra test**
- The new test also runs an `EXPLAIN` check that a wide table scanned
under a delim join CTE still projects only the columns it needs (`id,
pad1`), plus a result check on the same query. This confirms that
dropping the identity projections keeps column pruning.

**Results** (reldebug, before → after)

| query | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| lateral UNNEST + throwing filter, 4 GB limit | Out of Memory | 20 rows
counted, 0.34 s |
| `NOT EXISTS` + `json_valid` guard (range / unnest / json_each) |
Malformed JSON error | 2 |
| empty filter on view with lateral UNNEST, 3M rows | 0.012 s |
0.008–0.011 s |

Tests: the new test passes. `test/sql/subquery/*`, `test/optimizer/*`,
`test/sql/cte/*`, `test/sql/optimizer/*`, `test/sql/json/*` and
`test/sql/table_function/*` all pass (tpch/tpcds tests were skipped
because those extensions weren't in this build). The code isn't
clang-formatted, because there is no clang-format on the build box.

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
hunk_contexts: Value BuildDecimal(const duckdb_v2_hugeint_t *in_value, uint8_t width, uint8_t s
message:
Small fixes and additions to the stable C++ API (`tools/cpp`), found
while porting
[duckdb-odbc](https://github.com/Robinho-MR/duckdb-odbc/pull/1) from
DuckDB's internal C++ classes to `duckdb::cxx`. None of them changes the
C API or the engine.

### `StartupOptions::Set(name, value)`

`StartupOptions` only had five dedicated setters, while
`duckdb_v2_instance_create_with_options` accepts any option by name. So
the C++ API couldn't set any startup-only option that lacks a setter,
for example:
- `duckdb_api`, which every client sets to identify itself (the ODBC
driver sets `odbc`);
- `access_mode`;
- `extension_repository_directory`;
- any startup-only option a user puts in a connection string.

`Set` forwards a (name, value) pair to the C API, in the textual form
SQL `SET` accepts. Pairs are applied in the order given, after the
dedicated setters, so a later value wins. Options that need a running
instance (`allowed_directories`, ...) still go through
`Instance::GetConfig()`, as the C API documents.

### `Value::GetDecimal()` and a public `Value::CreateDecimal()`

`Value::Get<WIDTH, SCALE>()` and `Value::Create(decimal_t<WIDTH,
SCALE>)` need the width and scale at compile time. A driver learns them
at runtime, from a result column (`SQL_C_NUMERIC`) or a bound parameter
(`SQL_NUMERIC` with a precision and scale). Until now it couldn't read
the unscaled integer of a DECIMAL, nor create one, without going through
text.

- `Value::GetDecimal()` returns a `RuntimeDecimal {int128_t value;
uint8_t width; uint8_t scale;}`, through `duckdb_v2_value_get_decimal`.
- `Value::CreateDecimal(factory, int128_t value, width, scale)` was
already the private runtime forwarder of the typed constructor; it is
now public and documented.
- C API change: `duckdb_v2_value_create_decimal` now returns
`ERROR_INPUT_INVALID` for a value with more digits than the declared
width. Before, it only checked the storage tier, so e.g. 10000 at
`DECIMAL(4,0)` (or anything past 10^38 at width 38) built a value that
failed on bind or asserted in `ToText()`. INT16 and INT32 tier overflows
used to surface as an INTERNAL cast error; they are now
`ERROR_INPUT_INVALID` too.

### Compile when `<windows.h>` was included first

`<windows.h>` defines `DELETE` and `IGNORE` as macros. That turns the
`StatementType::DELETE` and `FunctionCollationHandling::IGNORE`
enumerators into syntax errors for any Windows consumer that includes it
before `duckdb_cpp.hpp`, which an ODBC driver must. The header now sets
both macros aside with `push_macro`/`pop_macro` while it is parsed.
These two are the only Windows macros among the header's enumerators.
Separately, `AddString` and `AddBlob` now call
`(std::numeric_limits<uint32_t>::max)()`, so the `max` macro (without
`NOMINMAX`) does not break them.

### Tests

New cases in `tools/cpp/tests` cover:
- startup-only options and aliases, override order, bad values and
unknown names;
- options that need a running instance;
- runtime DECIMALs across every storage tier, the typed constructor, a
query result, and out-of-range width, scale and value, plus non-DECIMAL
and NULL values.

`unittest "[cpp_api]"`: all 218 test cases pass (4248 assertions).
subject: C++ API: StartupOptions::Set, runtime DECIMAL access, windows.h compatibility (#28881)
title: C++ API: StartupOptions::Set, runtime DECIMAL access, windows.h compatibility

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
This PR fixes HTTP errors turning into JSON parse errors once the
per-host retry quota (#26947) refuses a retry. A failing httpfs read
then no longer reports the HTTP error, but `Serialization Error: Failed
to parse JSON string: {...}`, with the whole serialized HTTP error,
response headers included, as its message. For example, a range read
that keeps getting HTTP 429 from a rate-limited host fails this way
instead of with `HTTP 429 Too Many Requests`.

For requests that return their error instead of throwing
(`try_request`), `RunRequestWithRetry` keeps the error in
`request_error` and appends the quota exhaustion note to it. When the
request threw a DuckDB exception, or returned an error that holds one,
that string is the exception's JSON, so the note lands after the closing
brace. httpfs turns the request error back into an exception with
`ErrorData(response->GetRequestError())`, which parses anything that
starts with `{` as JSON and throws.

This PR appends the note to the exception message inside the JSON
instead, keeping the exception type and extra info, as the throwing path
already does. Plain text request errors get the note appended as before.

Could this get the `backport v2.0-cyanoptera` label? The retry quota is
in v2.0.0.
subject: Keep the HTTP error when the retry quota refuses a retry (#28920)
title: Keep the HTTP error when the retry quota refuses a retry

```sql
┌─────────┐
```

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
hunk_contexts: static bool CorrectSizeForBatch(const ColumnDataCollection &batch, const optiona
message:
A batched `COPY ... TO` given `ROW_GROUP_SIZE_BYTES` without
`ROW_GROUP_SIZE` fails:

```sql
SET threads=2;
CREATE TABLE t AS FROM range(1000000);
COPY t TO 'out.csv' (ROW_GROUP_SIZE_BYTES '256KB');
-- INTERNAL Error: Attempting to get the index of an optional_idx that is not set
```

`CorrectSizeForBatch` calls `batch_size.GetIndex()` without checking
that a row target is set. It is
reached for the leftover batch of a non-final repartition, so the error
depends on timing: the
query above failed on every run at 2 threads here (tested on Linux
x86_64; Apple ARM64).

With no row target, the byte target now decides, through
`CopyFunctionBatchAnalyzer::IsAcceptable()`,
as it does elsewhere. The new test
(`test/sql/copy/csv/batched_write/batch_csv_row_group_size_bytes.test`)
fails before the fix and
passes after.

## Demonstration

OSX using a fresh install of v2.0:

```bash
(base) 13:01:00 (dtmcdonald@when):~$ md5 /Users/dtmcdonald/.duckdb/cli/latest/duckdb
MD5 (/Users/dtmcdonald/.duckdb/cli/latest/duckdb) = b2fdfbcc753c7ad59e812516b4bb0c8a
(base) 13:01:03 (dtmcdonald@when):~$ /Users/dtmcdonald/.duckdb/cli/latest/duckdb
DuckDB v2.0.0 (Cyanoptera)
```

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
## Summary Enable adaptive min/max filtering of equality-join probe rows through shared machinery used by Parquet, native RLE, and DICT_FSST scans. The design separates two questions: - Does this value pass the filter? Cache that answer. - Is this optional filter saving work? Measure that from actual rows. Required predicates continue to apply when optional filters pause. ## Why this belongs in shared machinery A compressed entry can represent thousands of rows. Counting dictionary entries or runs therefore gives a different picture from counting actual rows. For example, two stored values might each appear once in a dictionary, while one represents almost every row. Evaluating the dictionary can suggest a useful filter even when it rejects almost nothing in practice. Native cached scans have this same problem as Parquet. They can also cache a temporary “accept everything” result when an adaptive filter is paused. Following the review feedback (https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/28515#issuecomment-6821426694), this change replaces the Parquet-specific min/max matcher with shared cache support. ## Implementation The shared implementation provides three guarantees: 1. Pure mask construction. Evaluate the underlying predicate without advancing adaptive counters or recording a paused pass-through result. 2. Feedback from actual row batches. Cached and fallback paths update the same per-filter state. Paused filters still advance their retry clock. 3. Independent mandatory filtering. Keep mandatory and optional results separate, preserving required predicates and evaluation order when optional filters pause. Caches are invalidated when their owning filter state expires. Unsafe predicates, unsupported adaptive expressions, and native segments requiring separate NULL validity use the existing row-evaluation fallback. ## Performance There will be - Before the fix - Original PR with min-max adaptive filter - Then the current after follow comments of reviewer ## The measured tradeoff comparing with original PR Keeping cached answers adds machinery, so we compared it with both the original PR and the simpler row-evaluation fallback. The table below shows earlier selective native-storage fixtures. A millisecond (ms) is one thousandth of a second. Lower times are better. The shared cache was about 36–38% faster than fallback, while costing about 3% for RLE and 6% for the string dictionary versus the original PR. There is a counterexample to a universal speedup: skewed native RLE was 13.7% slower than fallback. These were small warm tests before the upstream merge: 737,280 rows, one thread, 18 measured queries per image and case. Timings were not repeated after that merge. Deprecated change - reference as bellow
Equality-join min/max fallback filters currently prune Parquet row groups - But do not reject individual probe rows when groups overlap the build range. Then - **Enable adaptive row** evaluation and **keep scalar comparisons** on the **fast executor path**. Parquet measures actual row rejection outside dictionary-mask evaluation, keeps cached predicates deterministic, and preserves periodic pause/resume so an unrepresentative prefix cannot disable filtering for the whole group. Predicates proved exactly `ALWAYS_TRUE` skip evaluation. The specialized path accepts direct scalar ranges; other expression shapes use the existing evaluator. Regression coverage includes - Selective filtering within overlapping groups, - Recovery after a matching prefix, - Dictionary row-frequency feedback, - Mandatory predicates, NULL semantics and native scans. Validation: - TDD: the baseline emits 180,000 probe rows for 18,060 join matches. - The selective scan, recovery and dictionary-feedback regressions pass with the implementation. - Saved validation records for the rebased tree show 34 SQL comparisons, 17 native checks, and 183 assertions across five focused sqllogictest files (51 assertions in the three new regression files). These are targeted results, not a full-suite claim. - Scoped formatting and `git diff --check` pass; the optional local spelling tool was unavailable. - [Fork PR and CI results](https://github.com/kevintruong/duckdb/pull/2). T ## Parent-versus-head performance evaluation Re-evaluated - Upstream parent `6145a8699b5e54b146fb305a862012b58130e9b8` - Against PR head `0b6d5a35edeb9c9bd6d76233dffc29ff9a985eb1` - Using matching macOS arm64 compiler flags: `-O3`, assertions enabled, sanitizers disabled. - -The saved head runtime reports pre-amend build ID `7cd49cc31c`; its evaluated source blobs were verified against the final PR head. | Workload | Grounded finding | |---|---| | Selective join | Approximately 65% faster, about 2.9× speedup | | Broad and redundant-broad | Approximately 1.8% more executed instructions | | 90%-match | Instruction count essentially unchanged | | Native broad-match | No consistent slowdown established | The runs use the original issue's - 30-million-row probe fixture - Identical SQL/settings - And paired runtime order. Selective speedup is the paired geometric-mean estimate at two threads: - Head/parent time ratio `0.346` (95% bootstrap interval `0.324–0.370`). - Probe output falls from 30 million to 3.01 million rows while all 245 row groups are still scanned; this is not an I/O reduction claim. Controls use order-entry thresholds of 14 minutes (broad), 2,100 minutes (approximately 90% match), and 18,900 minutes (selective), with redundant probe predicates `ol_o_id >= 2` or `ol_o_id >= 2700`. Timing batches include 8 paired rounds and an independent 12-round confirmation with an identical-head-binary control; native and single-thread controls are also included. All 399 workload executions matched count/SUM checks, including 300 unprofiled timed queries and 24 profiles. Profiled runs did not spill. Instruction measurements are whole-process counts at one thread, with five queries per native process, including startup/setup. - Observed changes were `+1.815%` for broad, - `+1.814%` for redundant-broad, - And `−0.065%` for the 90% control. - - These percentages describe executed work, not wall-clock regressions. Related to #28269. AI-assisted implementation and validation.

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
An anti join whose preserved side is small and whose other side is large
("accounts in this region that have no event", `small EXCEPT big`, an
`ANTI JOIN` against a fact table) is flipped by the build side optimizer
into a RIGHT ANTI join: the small side is built, the large side probes.
The probe rows of a RIGHT ANTI join are never emitted, they only mark
build rows as matched, and the join returns the build rows that were not
marked. A probe row whose key does not occur on the build side cannot
mark anything, so it does not have to reach the join at all. That is
exactly the situation join filter pushdown exists for, and it already
handles RIGHT SEMI joins this way, but
`JoinFilterPushdownUtil::JoinTypeIsSupported` rejected RIGHT ANTI
together with ANTI ("FIXME: anti/right_anti - we could do this, but need
to invert the join conditions"). The inversion is only needed for a
plain ANTI join, whose unmatched probe rows are the result. For RIGHT
ANTI the build keys can be pushed into the probe side as they are.

This PR makes RIGHT ANTI a supported join type of join filter pushdown:

`JOIN_FILTER_PUSHDOWN` generates the filters (min/max, IN list, bloom
filter, as for any other join) for RIGHT ANTI comparison joins,
including the filters that are pushed into a materialized CTE on the
probe side.

With several equality keys the join gets the per-column bloom or
prefix-range filters of #28726 under the same condition as any other
join (build side at most 5% of the estimated probe side), and a scan
that #28768 lets wait for a small filter producer waits for a RIGHT ANTI
join as it does for a RIGHT SEMI join.

Plain ANTI joins stay unsupported. The choice of the build side is not
changed: `BUILD_SIDE_PROBE_SIDE` does not give RIGHT ANTI the dynamic
filter bonus it gives RIGHT SEMI. An ANTI join with a small filtered
preserved side is flipped by the size comparison already, and I found no
case in which the bonus alone decides the orientation (it needs a
preserved side that is at least 64 times smaller in rows than the scan
on the other side and still more expensive to build). Nothing changes in
the executor: the hash join already publishes its filters independently
of the join type.

### Preconditions

* the join is a RIGHT ANTI comparison join (i.e. an ANTI join that the
build side optimizer flipped);
* everything `JOIN_FILTER_PUSHDOWN` requires for the other join types:
the probe-side key expressions are not volatile, and the filter is only
pushed through operators and into scans that accept it.

The filters are part of `JOIN_FILTER_PUSHDOWN`: `SET disabled_optimizers
= 'join_filter_pushdown'` disables them together with all other join
filters.

### Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts AS SELECT i AS id, i % 50 AS region, i % 7 AS tier FROM range(2000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE events AS SELECT (i * 31) % 3000000 AS account_id, i % 365 AS day, i % 97 AS amount FROM range(60000000) t(i);

SELECT count(*) FROM accounts a ANTI JOIN events e ON a.id = e.account_id WHERE a.region = 7 AND a.tier = 3;
```

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, before:

```
HASH_JOIN    Join Type: RIGHT_ANTI; Conditions: account_id = id
  TABLE_SCAN events    Projections: account_id                                             60,000,000 rows
  TABLE_SCAN accounts  Filters: region = 7, tier = 3                                            5,714 rows
```

After:

```
HASH_JOIN    Join Type: RIGHT_ANTI; Conditions: account_id = id
  TABLE_SCAN events    Projections: account_id; Dynamic Filters: optional: account_id IN PRF(id)  114,280 rows
  TABLE_SCAN accounts  Filters: region = 7, tier = 3                                               5,714 rows
```

User-mode instructions at one thread (`perf stat -e instructions:u`,
median of 3, release build, `main` vs. this PR):

| query | main | this PR | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ANTI JOIN` (above) | 3.19e9 | 2.14e9 | 0.67 |
| `SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE region = 7 AND tier = 3 EXCEPT SELECT
account_id FROM events` | 3.18e9 | 2.13e9 | 0.67 |

A `NOT EXISTS` over the same tables does not change: it is decorrelated
into a different plan that already restricts the scan of `events`.

### Regression check

Without vs. with the change on TPC-H and TPC-DS (SF1 and SF10), JOB and
ClickBench: the results are identical at 1 and 32 threads (TPC-H /
TPC-DS SF1), and no `EXPLAIN` plan changes (join filters are not part of
the plan text, and no join changes sides). 3 of the 121 TPC-H / TPC-DS
queries have a RIGHT ANTI join; their instructions at one thread are
between 0.97x and 1.02x. There is none in JOB or ClickBench.

### Tests

`test/optimizer/pushdown/join_filter_pushdown_right_anti.test` (new):
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` pins that the probe scan of a RIGHT ANTI join gets
`Dynamic Filters` (also next to an inequality between the two sides),
that a plain ANTI join, a volatile probe key and `disabled_optimizers =
'join_filter_pushdown'` give none, and results for NULL keys on either
side with `=` and `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`, `NOT IN`, duplicate build
keys, two equality keys, VARCHAR keys, an empty probe side, an empty
build side, an anti join below an outer join, over an aggregate, over a
materialized CTE (one consumer, two anti join consumers whose filters
are combined, and an anti join next to an unfiltered consumer),
`EXCEPT`, and inside a recursive CTE. For joins on several keys it pins
the per-column filters (the same as for the RIGHT SEMI join, min/max
only above the 5% bound) and the results with NULLs in either key column
on both sides for `=`, `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` and a mix of the two, and
that a scan below an aggregate on the probe side waits for the filter
and the query still completes with an empty build side.

No existing expected plan changes. The tests in `test/optimizer`,
`test/sql/join`, `test/sql/subquery`, `test/sql/aggregate`,
`test/sql/optimizer`, `test/sql/cte`, `test/sql/setops`,
`test/sql/sql_export` and the TPC-H / TPC-DS SF1 answer tests pass,
`test/optimizer` and `test/sql/subquery` also with
`debug_verify_column_bindings` enabled.

#28732 converts more `NOT EXISTS` / `NOT IN` joins into ANTI joins
before join ordering, which produces more RIGHT ANTI joins for this
change to act on.

This PR is independent of the other optimizer PRs I am opening next to
it (#28786).

Note: this PR was generated by an AI coding agent; it is a draft pending
review by the author.

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
A plain CREATE of a repository that exists used to fail whatever it
asked for, so a script could not state "this repository, with this
definition" without IF NOT EXISTS (which keeps any definition) or OR
REPLACE (which overwrites). Now it returns the stored repository when
the request describes it, and names the difference otherwise:
- without a prefix the request only names a host, so it matches a
repository that was resolved from that host;
- with a prefix, the prefix must match (a trailing slash aside) and so
must the keys when the request gives any; keys that are not given were
fetched from the prefix and are not fetched again. Nothing here reaches
the network: what the host or the prefix serve today is checked only by
OR REPLACE. The strict "fail if anything is there" is still DROP without
IF EXISTS followed by CREATE.

The conflict is now decided before the opt-in
(allow_extension_repositories): returning what is stored adds no trust,
and a request for something else is reported as the difference it is,
whatever the access level. Only a statement that would add or overwrite
a repository is subject to the opt-in; a locked configuration still
refuses everything.

This makes that repeated:
```sql
CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY carlopi.github.io;
CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY carlopi.github.io;
CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY carlopi.github.io;
```
(same session or different sessions) succeed, and that allows script or
documentation pages to restate the `CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY` that
will double as assertion that stuff is (after a successfull statement)
properly set-up.

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
Closes https://github.com/duckdblabs/duckdb-internal/issues/11281

PR from https://github.com/duckdb-bot/duckdb/pull/107

Updating a `VARIANT` column with a nested JSON constant took time
quadratic in the nesting depth, and deeper values failed with `VARIANT
exceeds maximum recursion depth of 128`. Inserting the same value was
not affected.

The optimizer folds the cast into a `VARIANT` constant.
`RelationStatisticsHelper` then named each projection, group and
aggregate column with `GetName()`, and for an unaliased constant that
renders the value through `Value::ToSQLString`. Nothing reads these
names except `RelationManager::PrintRelationStats`, and nothing calls
that. This PR passes an empty `Identifier()` at the three call sites
instead.

At 64 levels, the `UPDATE` drops from ~11 s to 0.03 s on a release
build. The segfault in the JSON → VARIANT cast reported in the issue
does not reproduce on `main` anymore.

Tests:
- `test/optimizer/relation_statistics.cpp`: calls the projection and
aggregate statistics helpers directly with a 1,000-level constant, and
runs `UPDATE`, `first()`, `GROUP BY` and `INSERT ... SELECT` with it.
The SQL test is skipped in debug builds, because
`LogicalOperator::Verify` renders every plan expression there and fails

message:
Compressed materialization now resolves its casts through the database's
`CastFunctionSet`, like every other cast. User-registered casts apply
here too.

and `ValuePreservingCastFits` use the registered cast set. If a

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
When an `UPDATE` rewrites rows by deleting and re-inserting them, the
new rows are appended to the table. If one batch of rows didn't fit into
the current row group, the batch is cut down to only the rows that
spilled into the next row group, and the update then kept working with
that shortened batch. As a result, `UPDATE … RETURNING` silently
returned fewer rows than were updated. The fix slices the remaining rows
into a local chunk that references the input and leaves the input
untouched.

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
When a table is named like one of its STRUCT columns, the SQL that
DuckDB regenerates for an index on that column no longer binds. With
`CREATE TABLE s (s STRUCT(n INT)); CREATE INDEX idx ON s
((s.n::VARCHAR));`, `SELECT sql FROM duckdb_indexes()` (and so `EXPORT
DATABASE` and the `reparse_statement` verification) returns `CREATE
INDEX idx ON s((CAST(n AS VARCHAR)));`, which fails with a binder error
because the struct column reference lost its qualifier.

The cause is `RemoveTableQualificationRecursive` in
`CreateIndexInfo::ExpressionsToList`: it walks every column reference in
the index expression and strips the leading component whenever it equals
the table name, so the struct access `s.n` is treated as a
table-qualified column `n`. The transformer only ever adds the table
qualifier to a top-level, unqualified column reference (`CREATE INDEX
idx ON tbl (col)` is stored as `tbl.col`), while references inside
expressions are stored exactly as written.

This PR inverts only that step: the qualifier is removed from a
top-level two-component reference whose first component is the table
name, and expressions are left untouched. Verified with a new
sqllogictest that round-trips the regenerated statement, also under
`test/configs/verify_statement_to_string.json`, plus `test/sql/index/*`,
`test/sql/export/*` and `sqlite_master.test`.

author.

hunk_contexts: enum class StatisticsPropagationMode : uint8_t { FILTER_SIMPLIFICATION, FULL };
message:
With `debug_verify_stats` enabled, a filter with several conjuncts can
nondeterministically fail verification with `Statistics mismatch: value
is smaller than min` or `vector labeled as not having NULL values, but
vector contains null values`.
`StatisticsPropagator::PropagateStatistics(LogicalFilter &)` handles the
conjuncts one at a time, and each conjunct narrows the column statistics
(`UpdateFilterStatistics`) before the next one is propagated, so the
verification statistics attached to a later conjunct assume the rows the
earlier conjuncts reject are gone. `PhysicalFilter` ANDs the conjuncts
into one expression whose `AdaptiveFilter` reorders them after warm-up,
so a later conjunct is regularly evaluated over rows the earlier ones
would have rejected, and whether the check fires depends on the order
the adaptive filter happens to pick. 0f5722dc586 (#28275) fixed the same
thing for join conditions; this does the same for filter conjuncts.

The fix propagates all conjuncts once from the input statistics, which
attaches the verification statistics, and then runs the existing
per-conjunct pass (simplification, pruning, narrowing) with attaching
suspended through the `VerificationStatsGuard` the join code already
uses; the guard moves from `propagate_join.cpp` to
`statistics_propagator.hpp` so both can use it. The statistics derived
for the filter output and for pruning later conjuncts are unchanged.
`HandleFilter` gains an overload that takes the relation bindings
captured before the first propagation, so `FilterBindingsChanged` still
compares against the original expression.

Verification (reldebug): on main (5d254ad8707) the existing
`test/sql/optimizer/join_condition_verification_stats.test` fails 4 of 5
runs under `--test-config
test/configs/verify_statement_explain_sql.json`, whose SQL round trip
plans the join conditions as a filter; with this change it passes 10 of
10 runs plain and 10 of 10 under that config. The test gains the same
conditions written as a filter over a cross product, which fails 7 of 10
runs on main as a standalone script and 0 of 10 with the fix.
`build/reldebug/test/unittest
"test/optimizer/*,test/sql/optimizer/*,test/sql/filter/*,test/sql/join/*"`
passes.

unchanged physical plan. Filtered scans and scans feeding nested join

they can snapshot their filters before a small dimension build publishes

one vector. Keep the existing build/probe size guard, cycle checks, and

filtered nested build scan's cardinality with one and four threads, plus
prepared executions after changing and emptying the dimension.

| Total join output | 107,606 | 2,872 |
| Build input | 296,506 | 1,676 |
| Probe input | 190,121 | 2,843 |

physical plan and static filters were identical.

message:
Follow-up to duckdb/duckdb#28406, addressing duckdb-bot's review
(https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/28406#discussion_r4482331920):
dense selections through the new bitpacking `select` were slower than
the old scan + slice. The fix was pushed to the #28406 branch only after
#28406 had already merged.

Changes in `BitpackingSelect`:
- DELTA_FOR no longer decodes an algorithm group twice. `Skip` stops at
the start of the target's algorithm group instead of partially decoding
it, and after the last selected row the prefix sum continues to the end
of the already-unpacked group, so the next `Skip` doesn't unpack it
again for the carry.
- Dense selections (at least one selected row per 32-value algorithm
group on average) scan the range into a scratch buffer owned by the scan
state (at most one vector, allocated once per scan) and gather the
selected rows from it, since nearly every group is decoded anyway. This
is the old scan + select without the dictionary slice, which isn't
possible here because `result_offset` can be non-zero.

thread, min / median of 9 alternating runs. The box is shared and was at
load ~150 on 96 cores, so differences under ~5% are noise:

|---|---:|---:|---:|
| DELTA_FOR, `h < 16` (1 in 2 rows) | 301 / 323 ms | 352 / 366 ms | 313
/ 337 ms |
| FOR, `h < 16` (1 in 2 rows) | 282 / 302 ms | 305 / 324 ms | 301 / 322
ms |
| DELTA_FOR, `h = 31` (1 in 32 rows) | 301 / 306 ms | 313 / 325 ms | 293
/ 306 ms |
| DELTA_FOR, `id % 64 = 1` | 380 / 405 ms | 410 / 416 ms | 391 / 394 ms
|

| no filter (control) | 180 / 195 ms | 178 / 191 ms | 183 / 199 ms |

`list_sort` to repeat work. This broadens reusable dictionary output for
scalar payloads and enables it for small builds with `LIST` or `MAP`

dictionary emission because existing dictionary function execution can

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
Follow-up to #28656, which keeps the teardown of a query and the
scheduling of its tasks safe when an allocation fails. Sweeping the
malloc-failure shim of `tools/shell/tests/test_malloc_failure.py` over
every allocation boundary of a `SELECT 42` run (the test itself only
probes a handful of byte budgets, and the `test_malloc_failure_tail`
case is racy on CI, e.g. run 43172067810, "Linux Release Tests") found
one more place where the shell aborts instead of reporting
out-of-memory.

## Problem

**A joinable `std::thread` is destroyed while the pool launches its
threads (SIGABRT).** `TaskSchedulerPool::RelaunchThreads` started each
worker thread before it had a home: the `TaskSchedulerThread` wrapper
was allocated after `std::thread` was constructed, and the thread and
its cancellation marker were appended to two vectors that could still
reallocate. When any of those allocations failed, either the wrapper
holding the running thread was destroyed (`terminate called without an
active exception`), or `threads` already held the new thread while
`markers` did not, and the destroy pass of `~TaskScheduler` then failed
on `markers[i]` before it could join anything, so `~TaskSchedulerPool`
destroyed the joinable threads with the same result. On this machine
(192 hardware threads) that is a window of about 3600 consecutive
allocation boundaries during `DuckDB::DuckDB`.

## Fix

`RelaunchThreads` reserves `threads` and `markers` for the requested
thread count before the loop and creates the wrapper before the thread,
so once a thread runs, handing it to the pool cannot fail. An allocation
failure of the marker or the wrapper now stops launching further
threads, exactly like a failing `std::thread` constructor already did,
instead of leaving `RelaunchThreads` with an exception.

## Verification

All numbers are from the shim of `test_malloc_failure.py` on reldebug
builds (Linux aarch64, 192 hardware threads), failing every
malloc-family call from the N-th on, for every N in the given range; a
run counts as a failure when it neither exits 0 nor 1 with an
out-of-memory error.

| range of N | `main` (33e5799424b) | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 - 179999 (startup) | 1298 SIGABRT in `RelaunchThreads` /
`~TaskSchedulerPool` (N = 45119 - 48722), 244 SIGABRT at N <= 244
(static initialization, before `main`), 1 glibc TLS abort | 0 in
`RelaunchThreads` / `~TaskSchedulerPool`; the same 244 before `main` and
the same 1 TLS abort |
| 180000 - 320300 (query and teardown) | 7 glibc TLS aborts
(`GlobalUserSettings::GetSettings` on a worker, fixed by #28656), 2
SIGSEGV, 14 hangs | 5 TLS aborts, 2 SIGSEGV, 10 hangs (the same three
kinds, which depend on the thread interleaving) |

* `python3 -m pytest tools/shell/tests/test_malloc_failure.py
--shell-binary build/reldebug/duckdb`: 15 passed.
* `build/reldebug/test/unittest "test/sql/parallelism/*"` (79 test
cases) and `"[api]"` (682 test cases): all pass.

A release build of the same `main` commit gives the same picture for the
second row (142k runs: 38 hangs, 6 TLS aborts, 8 SIGSEGV, 1 heap
corruption in `~DatabaseInstance`, no `terminate`).

Observed but out of scope here: a SIGSEGV / heap corruption in
`DatabaseManager::ResetDatabases` during `~DatabaseInstance` after a
query was abandoned with out-of-memory, and the `main` entries of the
second row that #28656 addresses. An earlier sweep of a release build on
an older base also saw `std::bad_alloc` escape from `~ExecutorTask` on a
worker during teardown; that did not reproduce on this base in 140k-run
sweeps of either build type, and nothing in that destructor allocates
when profiling is off, so it is most likely the teardown use-after-free
that #28656 fixes.

No new test: which allocation fails first depends on the interleaving of
the worker threads, so the byte budget of the shim cannot select these
holes deterministically; the existing `test_malloc_failure.py` passes on
this branch and the sweep above is the coverage.

author.

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
Some aggregates keep their states in the arena but have no spill plan
(e.g. `quantile_cont`, `arg_max`, the `top-N` in h2o q08, `approx_top_k`
etc). Their memory can't shrink when the sink abandons, because
abandoning clears only the pointer table and the arena stays. Once the
arena alone is above the thread limit, Sink abandons on every chunk.
Each abandon re-creates the states of every repeated group in the arena,
so memory only grows. Going external doesn't help either, because it
can't release the arena.

This PR changes three heuristics, only for layouts without a spill plan:
- Abandon pressure: with a non-empty arena, abandon again only once the
HT's spillable part (everything but the arena) has grown by
`thread_limit / AGGREGATE_STATE_SPILL_DIVISOR` since the last abandon,
so re-created states don't trigger the next abandon.
- Going external: the decision ignores the arena, which stays in memory
either way.
- TryGrow: the arena doesn't count against the limit, and the cost of a
duplicate row includes its arena bytes.

Layouts with a spill plan or no arena take the old paths.

Release builds, threads=4 unless noted, median of 5 interleaved runs:

| query | before | after |

|-------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------|-----------------------|
| h2o q08, 500 MB | OOM after 68 s, 14 GB spilled | 0.39 s |
| h2o q08, 16 threads, 1 GB | OOM after 55–65 s, 12 GB spilled | 0.27 s
|
| quantile_cont, 1M groups, 1 GB | OOM after 82 s, 20 GB spilled | 0.88
s, 32 MB spilled |
| arg_max(v, v, 10), 1M groups, 1 GB | 0.90 s, 128 MB spilled | 0.75 s,
34 MB spilled |
| h2o q08, 300 MB | OOM after 27 s, 6 GB spilled | OOM after 0.7 s |
| 4 × approx_top_k, 200k groups, 16 threads, 2 GB | OOM after 106 s, 38
GB RSS | 10.0 s, 6.5 GB RSS |

This also happens at 1–2 threads. With 48-character string keys,
`quantile_cont` over 1M groups ran out of memory after 97–98 s and 23 GB
spilled, at both 1 thread / 500 MB and 2 threads / 700 MB. With this PR
it finishes in 1.7 s and 1.0 s.

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
Partial aggregate pushdown gives the new lower aggregate the estimate of
the aggregate above the join. That estimate is often the join estimate
itself, and it can exceed the lower aggregate's own input. The build
side optimizer then sees a huge aggregate and builds the other side of
the join instead.

Example, TPC-H q10 at SF3000:
- The lower `GROUP BY o_custkey` has 63M groups but was estimated at
1385M rows.
- So all 450M customer rows were built without a runtime filter.
- The top join took 156 instead of 24 thread-seconds.

The lower aggregate's estimate is now capped at both its input estimate
and the product of the current domains of its groups. The cap never
raises an estimate.

At SF1000 the only plan change is the build side of one join in TPC-DS
q74. The q10 case shows up with filter selectivity sampling (#28664),
whose estimates make the original estimate larger than the input.

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
The statistics propagator derives filters from inner/semi join bounds,
but previously lost them when the binder cast a column to the common
comparison type. For example, TPC-DS Q72 compares
`CAST(inv_quantity_on_hand AS BIGINT) < cs_quantity`, so the known
maximum of `cs_quantity` did not bound the inventory scan.

Derive these filters through invertible numeric casts using the existing
cast capability checks. This includes integer and decimal widening,
precision-safe conversions to floating point, and FLOAT to DOUBLE.
Convert each bound back with the built-in cast; inclusive bounds remain
conservative when conversion rounds, and the original join comparison
remains in place. Unsupported conversions and TRY_CAST are skipped, and
registered cast overrides retain their semantics. This stays within the
numeric types supported by join-statistics tightening.

The author's original integral-cast benchmark reported Q72 at SF1000
improving from 56 s to 1.5 s, and at SF3000 inventory input dropping
from 1.445B to about 139M rows. Those measurements predate the broader
numeric coverage.

Validation: the join-statistics suite (55 cases), cast optimizer suite
(9 cases), and three cast-pushdown tests pass with assertions and
float-cast-overflow sanitization enabled. All 540 differential queries
across 15 numeric type pairs match the previous PR head and
optimizer-disabled execution, including rounding, precision boundaries,
NaN, infinities, and NULLs. A 1M-row decimal-inequality microbenchmark
improves from a 99 ms median to 21 ms with identical results; IMDB and
TPC-DS were not rerun for this follow-up.

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
A plan that DuckDB versions before 2.0 serialized for a struct with a
`count(*)` field in a correlated subquery, for example `SELECT x,
(SELECT {'y': t.y, 'n': count(*), 'b': t.b} FROM o WHERE o.k = t.x) FROM
t`, no longer deserializes: "Failed to find function
struct_pack(VARCHAR,BIGINT,BOOLEAN)", which "takes no positional
arguments".

Plans written before v2.0.0 carry the argument names of `struct_pack`
only as the aliases of its arguments, and `RestoreNamesFromAliases`
takes the names from the trailing aliases, stopping at the first
argument without one. v1.x decorrelation (`RewriteCountAggregates`)
replaces the reference to the count with `CASE WHEN x IS NULL THEN 0
ELSE x END` without keeping the reference's alias, so that argument has
none and the arguments before it stay positional.

The fields of the recorded STRUCT return type are the argument names of
a v1.x `struct_pack`, so for a function that takes only keyword
arguments and returns a STRUCT with one field per argument, this takes
the names from the return type. The new `struct_pack_count_subquery`
case was serialized by v1.5.6.

This is a regression for plans written by v1.x, could it get the
`backport v2.0-cyanoptera` label?

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
A plan that DuckDB versions before 2.0 serialized for `approx_quantile`
over a DECIMAL column no longer deserializes: "Failed to find function
approx_quantile(BIGINT)", or another integer type, depending on the
DECIMAL's width.

In v1.x, `BindApproxQuantileDecimal` erased the quantile argument and
then replaced the whole function with the one for the DECIMAL's physical
type, which dropped `original_arguments`, so these plans record only the
shortened argument list. v1.x read them through a fallback in
`AggregateFunctionSet::GetFunctionByArguments` that took the first
overload whose leading parameters had the recorded types; #25991 removed
it. The existing `erased_arg_approx_quantile` case does not catch this,
because its DECIMAL call does carry original arguments.

For an aggregate in a plan written before v2.0.0 without original
arguments, when no overload matches, this selects the first overload
whose leading parameter types and return type match the plan and
completes the argument list with its remaining parameters. Matching the
return type keeps a scalar call from picking a list overload. The new
`erased_arg_approx_quantile_decimal` case was serialized by v1.5.6.

This is a regression for plans written by v1.x, could it get the
`backport v2.0-cyanoptera` label?
subject: Read v1.x plans of approx_quantile over DECIMAL (#28737)
title: Read v1.x plans of approx_quantile over DECIMAL

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
Projection placement moved each comparison of a column that other
expressions of the same projection also read, such as the `d_moy = 1` ..
`d_moy = 12` conditions of TPC-DS q66, below the joins onto the small
side. That frees no input column. It only adds one column per expression
that the joins have to carry.

When the small side is the build side of a hash join, these columns come
back as a global dictionary that every thread reads. The CASE
expressions above then contend on its shared validity buffer. At SF3000,
q66 took 1.19 s instead of 0.62 s.

With this PR, projection placement no longer moves an expression with a
heuristic cost of at most 20 (for example, a comparison of a numeric
column with a constant), unless moving it frees one of its inputs.

Of the 99 TPC-DS queries, only q66 changes plan. It only changes with
filter selectivity sampling (#28664): with sampling, q66 is otherwise
33% slower at SF1000 and SF3000, and this PR removes that regression.
subject: Do not move cheap projections below joins when their inputs stay needed (#28715)
title: Do not move cheap projections below joins when their inputs stay needed

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
A plan serialized by v1.x with a `MERGE INTO ... WHEN MATCHED THEN
UPDATE SET col = DEFAULT` on a table of a catalog other than DuckDB's
own, such as Iceberg or DuckLake, fails on 2.0 with "INTERNAL Error:
Attempting to initialize state of expression of unknown type!".

v1.x bound DEFAULT as a placeholder (BoundDefaultExpression), which the
update operator replaced by the default of the column when it ran. Since
#23033 the binder resolves defaults, but plans that still contain the
placeholder are supported: PhysicalUpdate resolves it. Since #25228 the
actions of other catalogs are planned through their regular
INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE planning. The SET expressions of an update action
are now evaluated in a projection before the catalog's update operator,
so the placeholder ends up in the projection, where it can't be
evaluated.

This PR replaces the placeholder with the bound default of its column
before the projection. It mirrors the deprecated branch that #25228 kept
for the insert action, which fills in the defaults of omitted columns of
v1.x plans.

Could this still be backported to v2.0?

title: Resolve SET col = DEFAULT of MERGE plans from before v2.0

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
hunk_contexts: static inline data_ptr_t InsertRowToEntry(atomic<ht_entry_t> &entry, const data_
message:
### Problem

`test/issues/general/test_27205.test` returns too few rows from a hash
join on the Windows 32-bit CI job, losing a varying number of build-side
rows between runs (one run returned 15733800 instead of 15734000,
another 15732800). It appeared after #28622 lowered the threshold for
building a join hash table in parallel to 65536 rows: the failing
query's build side has 78670 rows and the 4-core Windows runner now
inserts into the table from several threads.

The parallel insert loop reads entries with
`atomic<ht_entry_t>::load(std::memory_order_acquire)`. `ht_entry_t` is 8
bytes; on a 32-bit target the MSVC STL implements that load with
`__iso_volatile_load64`, which clang-cl (the compiler of the Windows
32-bit job) lowers to two 32-bit `mov`s. A thread can therefore observe
a half-written entry: the new pointer in the low half with the old salt
still zero in the high half. It treats the entry as occupied with a
non-matching salt, probes on, and starts a second chain for a key that
already has one; the probe later finds only the first chain and the rows
in the second one are silently dropped. With libstdc++ the same load is
a single `fildll`, which is why 32-bit Linux builds do not show the
problem; 64-bit targets load 8 bytes atomically.

### Fix

`LoadEntryConcurrent` reads an entry via
`compare_exchange_strong(expected, expected)` when a pointer is narrower
than an entry, which is a single `lock cmpxchg8b` and leaves the entry
unchanged; 64-bit targets keep the plain acquire load. The two loads on
the parallel insert path (the probe loop in `InsertHashesLoop<true>` and
the expected-entry load in `InsertRowToEntry<true, false>`) use it. The
single-threaded path is unchanged.

### Verification

- The torn load was confirmed by compiling the MSVC STL's 8-byte atomic
load with `clang++ --target=i686-pc-windows-msvc -O2 -S`: the load is
two 32-bit moves, the store likewise.
- 64-bit release build: `test_27205.test`, `test/sql/join/*` (205),
`test/issues/general/*` (130) and `test/sql/parallelism/*` (79) pass.
- 32-bit Linux build with gcc on an x86 machine: `test_27205.test`
passes 5/5 at 4 threads with and without the fix (libstdc++ loads
atomically), `test/sql/join/*` passes apart from an out-of-memory in an
ASOF slow test that fails identically without the fix (32-bit address
space; not run by CI).
- The Windows 32-bit job of this PR is the real check; main's nightly
passed that job once on 392cee07532, which is consistent with a race.

Note: this PR was generated by an AI coding agent and reviewed by the
author.
subject: Read join hash table entries atomically while other threads insert (#28682)
title: Read join hash table entries atomically while other threads insert

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
Supersedes #28381, fixes #28372 in a simpler way.

The PEG transformer merged `(A UNION B) UNION C` into one N-ary UNION
node, so the inner set operation never resolved its own result type and
`87::INTEGER` was cast straight to `VARCHAR` instead of through
`DOUBLE`.

`TransformSelectSetOpChain` now only merges into the N-ary nodes it
builds itself. A chain's first operand can only be a set operation when
it was written in parentheses (no other
`SelectAtom` alternative produces one), so such an operand stays nested
and the binder stages the cast through it. Unparenthesized chains are
unchanged and still become a single N-ary node.

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
Fixes #27759. This is #28623 by Yannick Welsch (his two commits
unchanged), plus one commit of extra tests.

### The fix (from #28623)

When the right side of a dependent join is a CTE that does not use the
domain, the CTE is moved above the join. Unless the join was a SINGLE
join with an uncorrelated left side, decorrelation then restarted the
whole join, so the left side was prepared twice. With a LIST correlation
(no duplicate elimination) that adds a second `row_number()` window
under the same table index, which fails with `INTERNAL Error:
Conflicting or cyclic column binding replacement`. The trigger repro
from #27759 goes the same way. The fix continues with the right side
after moving the CTE up, which is the path the SINGLE case already used.

### Also fixes a wrong result

The restart also gave silently wrong results for a CTE inside a nested
lateral join. On main this returns `2497 3666`, while the correct answer
(the same query written as a plain join) is `250 367`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE q AS SELECT i % 3 AS s, i % 4 AS k FROM range(200) t(i);
CREATE TABLE o AS SELECT i AS x, i % 3 AS g FROM range(10) t(i);
SELECT count(*), sum(n.k)
FROM o, LATERAL (SELECT * FROM (SELECT o.x) p,
                 LATERAL (WITH st(k) AS (VALUES (1), (2))
                          SELECT q.k FROM q WHERE q.k IN (SELECT k FROM st) AND q.s = o.g AND q.k < p.x)) n;
```

### Plan impact

I compared optimized plans on main and on this branch for LATERAL,
EXISTS / NOT EXISTS, IN, `> ANY`, scalar, LEFT LATERAL,
LIMIT-in-LATERAL, LIST, nested and stacked-CTE queries. They match,
except:
- the LIST and nested-lateral queries, which are the fixed bugs;
- two stacked independent CTEs (`WITH a AS (...), b AS (...)`). The
restart used to move both CTEs above the join; now only the first one
moves. `b` stays on the join's right side, but `PushDownCTE` leaves its
definition free of the domain, so it is still computed once. Results and
runtime were the same (about 2.05s at 20k x 2M rows).

### Extra tests in this PR

- the nested lateral wrong-result query above
- the two stacked independent CTEs
- removed `PRAGMA enable_verification` from the new test file

Could this get the `backport v2.0-cyanoptera` label? It is a v2.0
regression.
subject: Fix wrong results and "Conflicting or cyclic column binding replacement" when a lateral join reads a CTE (#28698)
title: Fix wrong results and "Conflicting or cyclic column binding replacement" when a lateral join reads a CTE

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
Fixes #27940.

The report’s query (a hash join of positions to rates, a CASE whose ELSE
branch is the build-side column fx_rate, and a selective filter on the
result) fails with INTERNAL "dict-surviving cache: global dictionary
column 1 changed identity after being seeded for dictionary caching" and
invalidates the database. The same happens with threads=1, with IF(...),
or with the branches swapped. With SET enable_caching_operators=false
the result is 31. The second reproduction in the report (CAST(JSON AS
VARCHAR)) already works on main, since the cache matches global
dictionaries by id.

The dictionary-aware operator cache (AppendToCache in
src/execution/physical_operator.cpp) pins a column’s global dictionary
on the first small chunk and accumulates selection indices for the
following chunks. If a later chunk carried a different dictionary or
none, a global dictionary threw, on the assumption that a producer emits
the same global dictionary for its whole lifetime. An expression above
the producer breaks that assumption: the CASE returns the join’s
dictionary vector unchanged for a chunk in which every row takes the
ELSE branch, a constant for an all-THEN chunk, and a flat vector for a
mixed chunk, so the filter’s cache saw the dictionary for some chunks
only. The hash join build already handles this on its side:
BuildColumnIsComputed treats a projection-computed column as one that
may arrive as a dictionary for some chunks only and does not narrow it.

The fix removes the throw and demotes the column to flat (materialize
the rows cached so far, then append flat). The cache has had that
demotion path for a rotating non-global dictionary, but only global
dictionaries are ever seeded, so it was never taken before. A flat
column is what the sinks receive without the cache. Other operators
forward a global dictionary for some chunks only as well (an external
hash join’s spilled probe rows come back flat, a cross product forwards
a column as a reference or as a constant depending on chunk sizes), so
the early check produced false positives for legitimate shapes. The hash
join build’s own checks still protect its row store.

Added test/sql/join/hash_join/dict_cache_computed_column.test (55
assertions): the report’s tables and query, IF, the swapped CASE,
sum/min/max of the demoted column, a GROUP BY sink, a VARCHAR dictionary
column, a switch between two global dictionaries from two joins, window
and ORDER BY LIMIT sinks, and a 500k-row case with threads=1 where two
dictionary columns go through several cache cycles and only one is
demoted and re-seeded. Expected values come from runs with
enable_caching_operators=false.

Verified on join (incl. hash_join), cte, aggregate, optimizer, filter,
parallelism, window, types/nested, subquery, projection and types/string
suites. The new test was run under disable_optimizer, verify_fetch_row,
force_external, vector_size_512, verify_serializer, shredded_vector,
verify_statement_prepare, verify_statement_copy and
disable_caching_operators.
subject: Demote a global dictionary column in the operator cache when its dictionary changes (#27979)
title: Demote a global dictionary column in the operator cache when its dictionary changes

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
Fixes https://github.com/duckdblabs/duckdb-internal/issues/11173

DETACH closes the database once `use_count() == 1`. But `use_count()` is
a relaxed load, so it doesn't synchronize with threads that already
dropped their reference without `close_lock`, e.g. a scanner that got
the database from `GetDatabases()`. TSan then reports a race between
their reads (`GetCatalog()`) and `Cleanup()`.

This PR copies our reference and drops the copy right before `Close()`:
- The decrement is acq_rel, so it synchronizes with all earlier
decrements of the counter.
- Dropping a copy rather than `attached_db` itself keeps the count at 1,
so we still close with the `checkpoint_on_detach` action instead of
through the destructor.
- This relies on `shared_ptr` decrements being acq_rel even when they
don't reach zero. That holds for all three standard libraries DuckDB
builds with (libstdc++, libc++, MSVC STL). An acquire fence would also
work, but TSan doesn't model fences.

The added test has a thread take a reference, read the catalog and drop
it, then runs DETACH. Without the fix it fails under TSan on every run.
subject: Synchronize with dropped references before closing a detached database (#28696)
title: Synchronize with dropped references before closing a detached database

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
`ColumnReader::block`, the buffer holding each page's decompressed data,
was previously allocated with an `Allocator` and was always kept pinned.

This moves `block` onto the buffer manager
(`BlockHandle`/`BufferHandle`), pinning it only around each vector's
read and unpinning it in between. `ByteBuffer` was changed to use an
offset-based cursor instead of an absolute pointer. Further, every
decoder that caches a pointer into `block` (dictionary, RLE,
delta-binary-packed, byte-stream-split) now rebases itself against the
new address after each re-pin.

One buffer was deliberately left on `Allocator`: the bloom filter built
while writing a dictionary page. It's short-lived and never re-pinned,
so buffer-manager tracking would only add overhead there with no
eviction benefit.

I ran a small benchmark locally, no speed regression, and it now keeps
working once memory gets tight enough that main just runs out of memory.

Also includes a small unrelated build fix in `expression_binder.cpp` I
hit along the way.

This looks like a lot of changes, but a lot of the changes are because
many of the functions were renamed for formatting reasons (ie. `inc()`
-> `Inc()`).
subject: Allow Pinning/Unpinning of ColumnReader::block (#25570)
title: Allow Pinning/Unpinning of ColumnReader::block

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
Since `AT TIME ZONE` on a `TIMESTAMP_NS` returns a `TIMESTAMPTZ_NS`,
comparing the result with a `TIMESTAMPTZ` fails to bind, while
`TIMESTAMP_NS` and `TIMESTAMP` compare fine:

```sql
SELECT (TIMESTAMP_NS '2026-10-12 12:34:56.123456789' AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') < now();
-- Binder Error: Cannot compare values of type TIMESTAMPTZ_NS and type TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE - an explicit cast is required
```

The same happens for `BETWEEN`, `COALESCE`, `IN` and list literals that
mix the two. They combine the types through an implicit cast in one
direction, and `CastRules::ImplicitCast` has no rule for a
`TIMESTAMP_TZ` source, so neither direction is allowed.

This allows `TIMESTAMP_TZ` to `TIMESTAMP_TZ_NS`, as `TIMESTAMP` already
casts implicitly to `TIMESTAMP_NS`, so the microsecond side is cast up.
On #28039 the different ranges of the two types came up as the reason
against this cast. `TIMESTAMP` and `TIMESTAMP_NS` differ in the same
way, and a `TIMESTAMPTZ` outside the nanosecond range now fails with the
same "Could not convert Timestamp to higher precision" that a
`TIMESTAMP` gets today. The cast also lets a `TIMESTAMPTZ` argument bind
to an overload that only takes `TIMESTAMPTZ_NS`, such as a `date_diff`
that mixes the two.

If that is acceptable, as a v2.0 regression, could this get the
`backport v2.0-cyanoptera` label?
subject: Compare TIMESTAMPTZ_NS with TIMESTAMPTZ without an explicit cast (#28672)
title: Compare TIMESTAMPTZ_NS with TIMESTAMPTZ without an explicit cast

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
## Fixes #28562

### Root Cause Analysis
- **File:** `src/optimizer/rule/empty_needle_removal.cpp`
- **Function:** `EmptyNeedleRemovalRule::Apply`
- **Lines:** The optimisation rewrites `contains(<non‑string>, '')` to a
constant `TRUE` because it only checks the return type (`BOOLEAN`) and
the needle type, but **does not verify the type of the first argument**.
This violates the invariant that optimisation rules must preserve
semantics for all overloads.

### Surgical Solution & Edge‑Case Safety
The fix inserts a guard that ensures the first argument is of type
`VARCHAR` before applying the empty‑needle rewrite. If the first
argument is not a string (e.g., `LIST<VARCHAR>`), the rule aborts,
leaving the original expression untouched. This restores correct
behaviour for `contains(list, '')` while keeping the optimisation for
genuine string overloads.

### Verification
- Run the DuckDB test suite to ensure no regressions: `make test`.
- Add a new test case (if not already present) that checks `SELECT
contains(["a", ""], '')` returns `false` (or `null` for a null list) and
that the optimizer does not replace it with a constant.
- Verify that existing string‑optimisation tests still pass.

---
*No other files are modified.*
